platforms.title: Easy Bruising After 60 Isn't Just "Old Age"
platforms.meta_description: Bruising easily on your hands and arms after 60 usually isn't just age. NIH data on actinic purpura explains the real mechanism and what actually helps.
platforms.body_html:
You catch your forearm on a doorframe, barely notice it, and two days later there's a dark purple blotch the size of a coin. Or worse — there's no bump you can remember at all. Most people file this under "I bruise easier now, I guess that's just getting older." That answer isn't wrong, exactly, but it's vague enough to be useless. There's a specific, well-documented mechanism behind it, a name for the condition, and three concrete things that change how often it happens. None of them involve giving up your morning aspirin.

It's Called Actinic Purpura, and It's Not Random

The medical name is actinic purpura (also called senile purpura or Bateman's purpura), and according to StatPearls, published by the U.S. National Library of Medicine at NIH, it's estimated to affect about 12% of adults over 50, rising to roughly 30% of people 75 and older. That is a specific, age-linked prevalence figure, not a vague "it happens to older people" statement.

The mechanism is mechanical, not circulatory. Collagen and elastic fibers in the dermis act as a support structure that holds small blood vessels in place. Decades of cumulative ultraviolet exposure — what dermatologists call photoaging — breaks that structure down fastest on the skin that has seen the most sun over a lifetime: the backs of the hands and the forearms. Once that support thins out, a vessel near the surface can rupture from something as minor as a tight sleeve or a light knock, with no memory of real trauma. Because there's no inflammation involved, the blood pools under the skin and clears slowly — StatPearls notes the patches typically resolve within 1 to 3 weeks without scarring, though a brownish stain from iron pigment can linger longer.

Your Aspirin Isn't the Cause — But It Isn't Helping

This is where most explanations get sloppy. Aspirin, warfarin, and clopidogrel don't create the underlying vessel fragility — the sun damage does that on its own. What these drugs do is make it harder for a vessel to stop bleeding once it has already torn, which is why bruises on blood thinners tend to run larger and darker. StatPearls lists corticosteroids and aspirin specifically as drugs that can exacerbate the lesions, and includes anticoagulant therapy in its differential diagnosis discussion for purpura generally. Long-term use of steroid creams compounds the problem by thinning skin through a separate pathway, on top of the sun damage that's often already there.

What Actually Changes When You Protect This Skin

None of this requires new medication or a dermatologist referral. Three ordinary habits address the three mechanisms directly:

  • Sunscreen, daily, not just at the beach. The American Academy of Dermatology recommends a broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher on exposed skin every day, regardless of season — properly applied, SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB rays. A long sleeve on a sunny errand does the same job for free.
  • Don't stop a blood thinner on your own. The clotting risk from quitting aspirin or warfarin without medical guidance is generally far more dangerous than the bruise itself. Instead, bring a current medication list to your next appointment and ask specifically whether the dose, or an alternative to a long-term steroid cream, is worth reviewing.
  • Moisturize daily, while skin is still damp. StatPearls notes that moisturizing creams may help with the skin dryness (xerosis) that often accompanies this condition. A plain, fragrance-free emollient applied right after washing works better than a specialty product used occasionally.

You Don't Need to Fix Everything at Once

The reassuring part: this is a benign, cosmetic condition, not a sign that something is failing internally, and none of the three fixes above require you to overhaul your routine overnight. Sunscreen and a moisturizer you already own cover two of the three causes; the third is just a conversation at your next checkup, not a decision to make alone at home.

What does deserve a same-week doctor visit: bruising that shows up on your torso or other skin that rarely sees the sun, bruising alongside fever or joint pain, or bleeding from your gums or nose that doesn't fit this pattern. Clinical guidelines from dermatology bodies reserve lab testing for exactly these atypical cases, precisely because ordinary actinic purpura doesn't need it. So: are the bruises you're seeing only on your hands and forearms, or are they showing up somewhere the sun never reaches?

This article is general health information, not a diagnosis — talk to a doctor or pharmacist before changing any medication.
